clue.text: Outlying part.

blocks.note: a plain definition: a district on the edge of a town

explanation.definitionFit: A residential district on the outskirts of a city lies out from its centre, so it is an outlying area.

clue.text: Where slowcoaches and old buffers meet.

definitions.text: Where slowcoaches and old buffers meet

blocks.note: the surface reading: dawdlers and doddering old men getting together

blocks.clueFragment: Where slowcoaches and old buffers meet
blocks.note: the setter's reading: slow railway coaches are shunted onto a short track that ends at buffer stops

explanation.walkthrough: A buffer is British slang for a foolish old man, and also the sprung stop at the end of a railway track.
explanation.definitionFit: A siding is a short side track off the main line where slow wagons are parked against the buffers.

clue.text: These produce a punch which may give the taster a rum feeling.

definitions.text: These produce a punch which may give the taster a rum feeling

blocks.clueFragment: a punch which may give the taster a rum feeling
blocks.note: the surface reading: a bowl of rum punch to be sampled
the setter's reading: the arm muscles that power a blow, and whoever tastes the blow feels odd

explanation.walkthrough: Punch is both the drink and the blow; 'rum' is British slang for strange, so the one on the receiving end feels peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: The biceps are the large upper-arm muscles that flex the elbow and drive a boxer's punch.

clue.text: Whatever their constitutional differences these always end harmoniously.

definitions.text: Whatever their constitutional differences these always end harmoniously

blocks.note: the surface reading suggests political states with different constitutions
the setter's reading: words of different make-up whose endings sound alike

explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutional' means how a thing is made up: the words differ at the front but agree in sound at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhymes are words whose final sounds match, so however different they are they finish in harmony.

clue.text: A regulation which shows how we are governed.

definitions.text: A regulation which shows how we are governed

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a rule made by a local authority or company

blocks.clueFragment: which shows how we are governed
blocks.note: split in two, the word says the manner of our government: through the law

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words the answer is 'by law', which is how a lawful state governs.
explanation.definitionFit: A bylaw is a regulation made by a local council or other body, applying within its own area.

clue.text: Note-with little more it could not be any less.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a musical note worth half a semibreve

blocks.clueFragment: with little more it could not be any less
blocks.note: add a couple of letters and the word becomes the one for the smallest possible amount

explanation.walkthrough: Add UM and MINIM becomes MINIMUM, which cannot get any lower.
explanation.definitionFit: A minim is the note lasting half a semibreve, called a half note in American usage.

clue.text: Inclined not to be strictly upright.

definitions.text: Inclined not to be strictly upright

blocks.clueFragment: Inclined not to be strictly upright
blocks.note: a plain definition, wordily put: leaning, at an angle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclined' tempts you towards a word for willing, but here it means tilted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something placed at a slope or slant leans off the vertical rather than standing straight.

clue.text: The year in yearly

blocks.note: the surface reading: happening once each year
the setter's reading: 'yearly' stands for its two-word Latin equivalent, and the year is the second of those words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yearly' stands for its Latin equivalent, per annum, and the year in that phrase is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Annum is the Latin word for year, used in English in per annum, meaning each year.

clue.text: It looks as though a sailor were in a mellow state here.

definitions.text: It looks as though a sailor were in a mellow state here

blocks.note: the surface reading: a seaman who has been drinking; the setter means an old salt, a sailor long at sea
the setter's reading: matured and softened by time, like wood or wine

explanation.walkthrough: The word starts with SEA, and seasoned also means salted, so it looks as though an old salt were in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Seasoned means matured or mellowed by time and use, and also experienced, as a veteran sailor is.

clue.text: Evidently a paragon of learning is one of looks also.

blocks.note: taken as written
a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge
taken as written

explanation.surface: Apparently the brainy model student is handsome too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evidently' points at the sentence itself: written out, 'a don is' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Adonis, the youth loved by Venus, stands for any strikingly handsome young man.

clue.text: States in which the head gets confused with the heart, with sensational results.

definitions.text: States in which the head gets confused with the heart, with sensational results

blocks.clueFragment: States in which the head gets confused with the heart
blocks.note: the surface reading suggests lovesick muddles; the setter means likings, where feeling rather than reason decides
the setter's reading: sensational in its old sense, to do with the senses, since one of the five senses shares the word

explanation.walkthrough: The crossings fix T?S?ES with the second and fourth letters unchecked; this is the reading that fits, a liking being a matter of heart over head and taste being a sense, but no key has confirmed it.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste for something is a liking or preference, decided by feeling, and taste is also one of the five bodily senses.

clue.text: The topic of how-do-you-do?

blocks.note: the surface reading: an everyday greeting, or a fuss
the setter's reading: the greeting literally asks after your health, so its subject is the science of keeping well

explanation.walkthrough: 'How do you do?' is taken literally, as a question about the state of your health.
explanation.definitionFit: Hygiene is the study and practice of keeping healthy, the very matter the greeting enquires about.

clue.text: A tripping foot, but no penalty is imposed for its use.

definitions.text: A tripping foot, but no penalty is imposed for its use

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a metrical foot with a light, skipping rhythm, one long syllable and two short

blocks.clueFragment: but no penalty is imposed for its use
blocks.note: the surface reading: a foot that trips an opponent in football would be penalised

explanation.walkthrough: The football picture is the misdirection; the foot is a unit of verse, as in 'MERrily, MERrily'.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody this is the foot of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones, which gives verse a tripping movement.

clue.text: These old plutocrats are at least blest with a few shillings.

definitions.text: These old plutocrats are at least blest with a few shillings

blocks.note: the setter's reading: men who came home rich from India in the eighteenth century

blocks.clueFragment: are at least blest with a few shillings
blocks.note: the surface reading pokes fun: the word ends in 'bobs', slang for shillings, so such men at least have a few

explanation.walkthrough: A bob was British slang for a shilling, an old coin worth a twentieth of a pound; the joke is that the word's tail reads 'bobs'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nabob was a European who made a great fortune in India and returned to flaunt it, hence any very rich man.

clue.text: Most superior.

blocks.note: a plain definition: the Latin superlative for greatest

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Latin, familiar from titles such as Pontifex Maximus.
explanation.definitionFit: Maximus is Latin for greatest, the highest degree of being superior or great.

clue.text: Blessings.

blocks.note: a plain definition: strokes of good fortune to be thankful for

explanation.definitionFit: Mercies are things to be grateful for, as in 'thankful for small mercies'.

clue.text: A young man with expectations, relatively speaking.

definitions.text: A young man with expectations, relatively speaking

blocks.note: the surface reading: a hopeful youth, perhaps due an inheritance
the setter's reading: speaking in terms of relatives, he is a family member who may inherit from an uncle or aunt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relatively speaking' is the pun: it points to a family relation rather than meaning 'comparatively'.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's son is a male relative who traditionally hoped for a legacy from a childless uncle.

clue.text: A timely word which seems to have gained the ear of a late-riser.

blocks.note: taken as written
one who lies in bed late in the morning

explanation.surface: A well-timed word of advice manages to reach someone who sleeps in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gained the ear of' sounds like winning someone's attention, but the word literally has EAR joined to one who lies in.
explanation.definitionFit: Earlier is a word about time, meaning at a sooner hour, just what a late riser is told to be.

clue.text: This, too, gained the ear of a king, but with tragic results.

definitions.text: This, too, gained the ear of a king, but with tragic results

blocks.clueFragment: gained the ear of a king
blocks.note: the surface reading: a counsellor winning royal favour
the setter's reading: in Hamlet, Claudius pours a poison into the sleeping king's ear

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's father was killed with 'juice of cursed hebenon' poured in his ear, usually taken to be this plant. 'Too' links it to the clue above.
explanation.definitionFit: Henbane is a poisonous plant of the nightshade family, identified with the poison in Hamlet.

clue.text: Just note when you take a rise out of it.

definitions.text: Just note when you take a rise out of it

blocks.note: the surface reading: simply take notice; the setter's reading is 'only a short written note'

blocks.clueFragment: when you take a rise out of it
blocks.note: the setter's reading: 'take a rise out of' usually means tease, but here a word for rise is lifted out of the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Remove RISE from MEMORISE and MEMO is left, which is 'just [a] note'. 'Take a rise out of' normally means to tease someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To memorise something is to commit it to memory, a way of firmly noting it in the mind.

clue.text: Contribute.

blocks.note: a plain definition: to add to

explanation.definitionFit: Something that redounds to your credit contributes to it, adding to your good name.

clue.text: The tables here are certainly habitable.

definitions.text: The tables here are certainly habitable

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the clue word tables sits inside the answer, with one letter before it
the surface reading sounds like house-hunting; the setter means buildings where horses are lodged

explanation.walkthrough: Put S before TABLES and you have the answer, buildings that certainly have residents, of the equine kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Stables are buildings where horses are housed and fed, lived in by their animal tenants.

clue.text: Thus wise men when it comes to talking.

definitions.text: Thus wise men when it comes to talking

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the letters of the word for wise men, SAGES, set out in a different order
the surface reading: how the wise behave in conversation; the setter means that to gas is to talk idly at length

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the sages, put another way, only gas. To gas is informal for chattering emptily.
explanation.definitionFit: Gases, as a verb, means chatters or talks idly, the opposite of what wise men are supposed to do.

clue.text: Eastern garment that might suit an incendiary.

blocks.note: first meaning: a hooded cloak worn by Arabs and Berbers
second meaning, a pun: the word starts with burn, so it would suit someone who sets fires

explanation.walkthrough: An incendiary is an arsonist; the cloak's name begins with the very thing he does.
explanation.definitionFit: A burnous is the long hooded cloak of North Africa and Arabia.

clue.text: Scenes of prolonged sittings shortly.

blocks.note: the surface reading suggests long sessions of a parliament or a court; the setter means hens brooding on eggs
the setter's reading: put briefly, in one short word

explanation.walkthrough: A sitting hen stays on her eggs for weeks; the places she does it are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds build nests and sit on their eggs in them for the long period of incubation.

clue.text: Here an old enemy develops an idea and finishes with the hump.

blocks.clueFragment: Here an old enemy develops an idea
blocks.note: the setter's reading: the old enemy is the Hun, a First World War name for the Germans, and the Hun grows into a hunch, an idea
the setter's reading: the word then ends up describing someone bent with a hump

explanation.walkthrough: The clue tells a little story of a word growing: HUN, then HUNCH (a hunch is an intuition), then HUNCHED. 'The hump' also means a sulk.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunched means bent over with the back humped up, as a hunchback is.

clue.text: Tony Weller seems to have thought it indispensable.

definitions.text: Tony Weller seems to have thought it indispensable

blocks.note: the setter's reading: Sam Weller's coachman father in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

blocks.clueFragment: seems to have thought it indispensable
blocks.note: at Mr Pickwick's breach-of-promise trial he bellows that there should have been one of these, as the only real defence

explanation.walkthrough: In Pickwick Papers, as the trial goes against Pickwick, old Tony Weller cries 'Vy worn't there a alleybi!'
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is the plea that the accused was somewhere else at the time, which Tony Weller saw as the defence nobody should be without.

clue.text: A queen who neglected her laundry and gave a name to a colour.

definitions.text: A queen who neglected her laundry and gave a name to a colour

blocks.clueFragment: A queen who neglected her laundry
blocks.note: the setter's reading: the royal said to have vowed not to change her linen until a siege was won

blocks.clueFragment: gave a name to a colour
blocks.note: her soiled underclothes supposedly named a greyish-yellow shade

explanation.walkthrough: Legend says the Archduchess Isabella vowed not to change her shift until Ostend fell; the siege lasted three years, and isabelline is the dingy yellow that resulted.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella is the royal of the legend behind isabelline, a pale greyish-yellow colour.

clue.text: In hesitation a bee quietly breaks out.

definitions.text: In hesitation a bee quietly breaks out

blocks.note: the setter's reading: someone hesitating is in a state of uncertainty, and that state is the answer
the surface reading is of an insect escaping; the setter means the letter B sits in the word but is silent

explanation.walkthrough: 'A bee' is the letter B, and 'quietly' says it is not sounded: the B in the answer is written but never spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Doubt is uncertainty, and to be in doubt is to hesitate over what to believe or do.

clue.text: The same as below, but also far apart.

blocks.note: first meaning: in the way set out underneath
second meaning: into separate pieces, divided

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer after two letters and it reads 'as under', an old way of writing 'as below' in a document.
explanation.definitionFit: Torn asunder means pulled apart into pieces, separated widely from one another.

clue.text: Medicinal leaf.

blocks.note: a plain definition: dried leaves of the cassia plant, used as a laxative

explanation.definitionFit: Senna is the dried leaflets and pods of cassia shrubs, long taken as a purgative remedy.

clue.text: A valley in which you'll meet with, verminous company.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a broad river valley in Scotland

blocks.clueFragment: in which you'll meet with, verminous company
blocks.note: a rodent sits in the middle of the word

explanation.walkthrough: The word holds RAT in its middle. A strath is the Scots word for a wide valley, as in Strathspey.
explanation.definitionFit: A strath is a broad flat river valley in the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: Sunder (anag.).

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the abbreviation tells the solver outright that the letters of the word before it are to be put in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be reordered, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: A bare anagram with no definition, as early Times puzzles sometimes gave; the crossings settle which word is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Nursed means tended the sick, or cradled and cared for something carefully.

clue.text: We also fly and escape recapture (hidden).

indicators.note: the setter states outright that the answer lies concealed in the run of the clue's own words

blocks.note: the answer runs across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third
surface padding: it completes the picture of a getaway and gives no letters

explanation.surface: Some captured creatures say they can fly too, and will get away again.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter gives no real definition: 'We' is the answer speaking, a range of mountains, and the rest of the sentence is surface. The bracketed note is the only signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are the long mountain range of western South America, here the 'we' who speak the clue.

clue.text: This province has the best card.

blocks.note: the setter's reading: a region of eastern France on the Rhine
the word holds the top card of a suit at its end

explanation.walkthrough: The word ends in ACE, the highest card in most games.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsace is the historic province of north-eastern France between the Vosges and the Rhine.

clue.text: This may hold you up.

blocks.note: a plain definition with a pun: not support you but delay you

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold you up' looks like propping up; it means keeping you waiting.
explanation.definitionFit: To detain someone is to hold them back or keep them from going, delaying them.

clue.text: Shows where you stand.

blocks.note: a plain definition: your position or rank relative to others

explanation.definitionFit: Status is a person's standing or position in society, so it tells you where you stand.

clue.text: Tube rule (anag.).

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the abbreviation tells the solver outright that the letters of the two words before it are to be put in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be reordered, taken as written

explanation.surface: A bare instruction: a rule for the Underground, with its letters to be reworked.
explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles sometimes gave a plain anagram with no definition at all; the crossings confirm which word is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: True blue means staunchly loyal, especially to the Conservative party, whose colour is blue.

clue.text: Priest.

definitions.note: the clue is singular but the grid's answer is the plural

blocks.note: a plain definition: a Buddhist monk of Tibet

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'Priest', yet the crossing letters need the plural, so the setter slipped on number.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamas are the monks and spiritual teachers of Tibetan Buddhism, its priestly order.

clue.text: A slight alteration makes those look customary.

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, the customary spirit of a people, not an adjective

indicators.note: altering the word slightly suggests its letters are shifted into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A small tweak is enough to make some things look ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter moves, the E from the end to the front, which is the 'slight' alteration.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethos is the characteristic spirit and habits of a group, its customary outlook.

clue.text: A genuine antique.

definitions.note: the clue reads as a noun phrase; the answer is the superlative adjective

blocks.note: the surface reading: a real piece of old furniture or china
the setter's reading: the truly antique thing is the one of greatest age

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is thin: a genuine antique is meant to be the most aged of all, so the answer is the superlative of old.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldest means of the greatest age, which is what makes an antique authentic rather than a reproduction.

clue.text: The way of the world.

blocks.note: the surface reading: how things usually go in life
the setter's reading: the path the Earth travels around the Sun

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means ordinary life; taken literally, it is the planet's path through space.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbit is the curved path a planet follows around the Sun, so the world's way through space.

clue.text: The flowers in these seasons are surely hardly in season.

definitions.text: The flowers in these seasons are surely hardly in season

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the lilies and other blooms used to decorate churches at a spring festival
the surface reading teases: the festival falls so early in spring that its flowers must be forced

explanation.walkthrough: The joke plays on 'seasons' twice: church festivals and times of year. Easter lilies were grown under glass to be ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Easters are the yearly Christian festivals of the Resurrection, held in early spring when few flowers bloom naturally.

clue.text: Archbishop of Canterbury who was canonized.

definitions.text: Archbishop of Canterbury who was canonized

blocks.clueFragment: Archbishop of Canterbury who was canonized
blocks.note: a plain definition: the Italian-born theologian who held the see under William II and Henry I

explanation.definitionFit: Saint Anselm, archbishop from 1093 to 1109, was canonised and named a Doctor of the Church.

clue.text: This salt is not recommended for table purposes.

definitions.text: This salt is not recommended for table purposes

blocks.note: the surface reading: a kind of seasoning; the setter means only that the word ends in salt

blocks.clueFragment: is not recommended for table purposes
blocks.note: the setter's reading: it is a hard volcanic rock, so nobody would sprinkle it on food

explanation.walkthrough: Only the last four letters make it a 'salt'; the whole is a dark igneous rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Basalt is the dark, fine-grained volcanic rock of lava flows, nothing like table salt despite its ending.

clue.text: You'd expect a strong silent man to be.

definitions.text: You'd expect a strong silent man to be

blocks.clueFragment: You'd expect a strong silent man to be
blocks.note: a plain definition by description: what the strong silent type is, sparing of words

explanation.walkthrough: The ancient Spartans of Laconia were famous for their curt speech, which gave the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic means using very few words, the terse manner expected of the strong silent type.

clue.text: Two heads are not better than one here.

definitions.text: Two heads are not better than one here

blocks.clueFragment: Two heads are not better than one
blocks.note: the surface reading twists the proverb 'two heads are better than one'
the setter's reading: monsters for which every head cut off grows two in its place, so two are worse for the hero

explanation.walkthrough: Hercules fought the Hydra of Lerna, which sprouted two new heads for each one he cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydras are many-headed serpents of Greek myth, whose heads multiplied when severed.

clue.text: A game much patronized by Royalty in the past.

definitions.text: A game much patronized by Royalty in the past

blocks.note: the surface reading: any sport or pastime

blocks.clueFragment: much patronized by Royalty in the past
blocks.note: the setter's reading: the indoor court game played by Henry VIII at Hampton Court

explanation.walkthrough: Real tennis, the original indoor game, was a pastime of French and English kings.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis began as the royal court game of medieval and Tudor monarchs before the lawn version appeared.
